subsections.subsection_title: How to present a NORMAL neurological examination

blocks.text: “On neurological examination, the child is alert and appropriately interactive for age. Cranial nerves are grossly intact. There is normal muscle bulk and tone with normal and symmetrical power. Deep tendon reflexes are present and symmetrical, with flexor plantar responses. Sensation is intact where assessed. Coordination is normal and gait is appropriate for age. There are no abnormal involuntary movements or signs of meningeal irritation.”

“The infant is alert and appropriately interactive for age, with symmetrical spontaneous movements and appropriate posture. Cranial nerve function is grossly intact. Tone is appropriate, with symmetrical primitive reflexes appropriate for age. Deep tendon reflexes are present and symmetrical, with no focal neurological deficit identified.”

“The child is alert and interactive. There is reduced spontaneous movement of the right upper and lower limbs. There is increased tone and power is reduced on the right, with brisk deep tendon reflexes and an extensor plantar response on the right. The findings are consistent with a right-sided upper motor neuron syndrome.”
“Depending on the pattern and associated findings, the lesion could involve the left cerebral hemisphere, corticospinal tract or another part of the central motor pathway.”

“The child has a broad-based unsteady gait with dysmetria on finger-nose testing and impaired rapid alternating movements. There is no significant weakness or sensory deficit. These findings suggest cerebellar dysfunction.”

Before you leave the station, ask yourself:

Did I assess consciousness? Did I observe spontaneous movements? Did I examine cranial nerves? Did I assess tone? Did I assess power/function? Did I check reflexes and plantars? Did I assess sensation where appropriate? Did I assess coordination? Did I watch the gait? Did I look for meningism? Did I adapt the examination to the child's age?

content_groups.group_title: ⭐ The most important pediatric neurological principle

blocks.text: Don't just perform manoeuvres—interpret the child as a whole.
A child with neurological disease may reveal the diagnosis through development, posture, spontaneous movement, tone, gait and behaviour before you perform a single formal neurological test.
